doc.title: Mat Domber interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2007

title: Kenny Davern's death and his Pee Wee Russell connection
summary: Domber recalls Davern's sudden death, his own year of clarinet, and becoming friends with Davern.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Who were the great clarinetists? Favorites and rivals

blocks.x: I know that we were all really shocked when Kenny died. He was a big part of your label for sure. Was there something in particular that you liked about his playing?

Well yes, almost everything. Yeah Kenny’s death came as a great shock. As a matter of fact we have a record that’s going to be coming out very shortly, that we recorded a while ago in 2005 actually, of Kenny and Ken Peplowski. And just the day before he died he was talking with my assistant Claudia. Dan Morgenstern has written the album notes for the CD and he was just talking with her about some changes that he wanted or suggested in the notes. And no, there was no premonition that he had a heart problem or anything else. He just, at ten o’clock one night, the next night he complained of pains in his chest and within an hour he was dead. But my initial attraction with Kenny came from the fact that I knew that he was one of the legatees of Pee Wee Russell. And even before I got to know Kenny personally, Pee Wee Russell was one of my idols. When I was 13 years old

I studied the clarinet for one year and I used to sit on the edge of my bed in the room trying to emulate Pee Wee Russell’s solos and the sounds and the croaking sounds that he made. And when I realized that I didn’t have the talent to be able to do that I gave up the clarinet after one year. That was it. That was my whole musical education in one year. But I knew, for example, that Kenny Davern was a good friend and that Pee Wee in some ways was a mentor to him and that he inherited Pee Wee’s clarinet and so there was, I felt, a certain initial bond that I had to Kenny before I even knew him or anything else. And of course I’d heard a lot of his records and such and knew about him. And when we had the chance to have him perform at our first March of Jazz party in 2004 that’s where I really started to get to know him and Bob Wilber both. And we discovered — I discovered that he was a man who was not only a consummate musician but he was a very interesting person besides. He had a world of knowledge about a lot of subjects. He read extensively. He delved into classical music and into opera and he was a man of decided likes, dislikes and opinions.
And we became very good friends. And I considered it a great pleasure and an honor to be able to record him.
